claim: Zionism is a colonial project that stole the land.

heard.who: Lorenzo Veracini, historian of settler colonialism, in a 2022 interview
heard.quote: Zionism is a settler colonial movement and Israel is a settler colonial state. This is not an insult; it is a statement of fact.

answer: Zionism's founding text, the Basel Program of 1897, says its aim is 'a home in Palestine secured by public law' for the Jewish people, to be reached partly by settling Jewish farmers and workers there. Herzl called it the restoration of the Jewish state, and he and his successors used the word 'colonization'. But Zionism was never one thing: political, labour, religious, cultural and revisionist Zionists differed, and bi-nationalists such as Brit Shalom wanted Jews and Arabs to share the country. Many Jews opposed it: the Bund, Reform rabbis, and the Orthodox Agudat Israel. Scholars disagree whether 'settler colonialism' describes it. Khalidi, Wolfe and Veracini say yes; Dowty says there was no mother country and the settlers were largely refugees.

facts.text: Some Zionists wanted a state shared by Jews and Arabs. Berit Shalom, founded in Jerusalem in 1925, proposed a bi-national solution with Jews and Arabs having an equal share in the administration regardless of their numbers; it never had more than 200 members, and Martin Buber and Judah Magnes were its best-known supporters.

facts.text: Many Jews opposed Zionism before 1948: the secular socialist Bund was 'uncompromisingly anti-Zionist', the Reform rabbis' conference said Jews were 'at home' wherever they lived, and the Orthodox Agudat Israel opposed any attempt to revive Jewish nationhood in the land by human action.

contested.text: Position: Zionism is settler colonialism. Rashid Khalidi says the early Zionists used the language of colonisation themselves and that the movement took over land from Palestinians. Lorenzo Veracini says the lack of a single mother country shows only that Zionism was not 'colonial' in the imperial sense, not that it was not settler colonial. Patrick Wolfe's general theory, which writers such as Khalidi and Veracini apply to Zionism, is that settler colonizers come to stay, so that invasion is a structure and not an event.

sources.title: Rashid Khalidi on Settler-Colonial Israel: An Interview
sources.quote: none of them made any bones about the fact that they were doing this as part of a settler colonial process

contested.text: Position: the description does not fit. Alan Dowty, a political scientist, says classic colonialism needs a metropole, a mother country whose agents the colonists are, and that there was none; he adds that most Jews who came were refugees fleeing persecution and not agents of a sponsor. Supporters of the description answer that a settler movement needs no single mother country, and that historical ties to the land do not remove the question of the people already living there. This card reports the argument; it does not decide it.

could_not_verify: Jewish opposition to Zionism 'now' (for example Haredi groups such as Satmar, or Jewish Voice for Peace): I found no reliable readable page and cover only the pre-1948 opposition.

Derek Penslar's position (Zionism as a hybrid of colonial, anti-colonial and national movement) and Troen's: I found only summaries of them, not their words on a readable page, so they are not quoted.
Avalon's text of the Basel Program did not load; the quote is from other sites, and the translations differ in small ways ('public law', 'publicly and legally assured').
The word 'colonization' in the Basel Program is in the COJS translation; the Encyclopaedia Judaica gives 'settlement'. I did not find the German original on a readable page.
Herzl's own use of the word 'colony' and the Jewish Colonization Association: Khalidi mentions it but I found no readable primary page.
Wolfe's own application of his theory to Zionism (his book Traces of History) was not readable; I quote only his general statement of the theory.
not_claimed: This card does not decide whether 'settler colonialism' is the right label; it gives both sides.
It does not say Zionism was a single movement with a single aim, or that all Zionists sought a state shared with Arabs or a state alone.
It does not say the Basel Program ruled out an Arab presence; it is silent on the people already living there.
It does not claim the opposition to Zionism among Jews was only religious or only socialist; the sources named give three kinds.
